name: American Grotesk
classification_notes: Lineal grotesque revival rooted in Morris Fuller Benton's Franklin Gothic (1902) and its siblings – News Gothic and Lightline Gothic. Preserves the original's medium stroke contrast, short cap extenders, angled terminals and asymmetric C bite. Three widths (Normal, Condensed, Compressed) are unified into a single coherent family for the first time, totalling 42 styles.
summary: Kris Sowersby's 2024 revival of Franklin Gothic, consolidating the Benton grotesque tradition – Normal, Condensed and Compressed – into 42 styles across seven weights with matching italics.
description: American Grotesk draws from Morris Fuller Benton's Franklin Gothic (1902) and its siblings – News Gothic and Lightline Gothic – unifying their disparate proportions into a coherent family for the first time. Three widths span seven weights each, with matching italics, totalling 42 styles. Key characteristics of the original are preserved: medium stroke contrast, short cap extenders, angled terminals and the asymmetric C bite, alongside alternate glyphs that honour the wood type heritage.
foundry_blurb: Rooted in Franklin Gothic and the broader Benton grotesque tradition, American Grotesk was developed against a backdrop of contested truth and generative AI – fonts built from the visual language of American persuasive communication, reassembled for a culture of personal truth-making. The design consolidates what Benton left scattered, treating News Gothic and Lightline Gothic as intended lighter companions to the original rather than separate families.

name: American Grotesk Compressed
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Lineal: Grotesque; the most compressed width in the American Grotesk system, rooted in Franklin Gothic and the wider American vernacular.
summary: The most compressed width of American Grotesk, built for posters and mastheads where every millimetre of horizontal space counts.
description: A compressed grotesque by Kris Sowersby that takes the American Grotesk system to its narrowest setting. Fourteen styles run from Thin to Black with matching italics, and the family connects to the standard and Condensed widths so editorial systems can flex from body to billboard. The Woodtype stylistic set hints at the American poster heritage Klim describes for the wider family.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify American Grotesk Compressed as Lineal: Grotesque, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2024. It is the compressed width within the American Grotesk system, sharing the family's Franklin Gothic reprisal and its grounding in American graphic vernacular and persuasive communication.

name: American Grotesk Condensed
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Lineal: Grotesque; the condensed cut within the American Grotesk system, drawing on Franklin Gothic's role in American graphic vernacular and persuasive communication.
summary: The condensed cut of American Grotesk, holding Franklin Gothic's voice at tighter measures for headlines, posters and packaging.
description: A condensed grotesque by Kris Sowersby that compresses the American Grotesk system without losing its Franklin Gothic accent. Fourteen styles span Thin to Black with matching italics, sitting between the standard width and the tighter Compressed cut. Reach for it on posters, mastheads and packaging where you want vertical economy and the same vernacular American voice.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify American Grotesk Condensed as Lineal: Grotesque, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2024. It is the condensed width within the American Grotesk system, sharing the family's reprisal of Franklin Gothic and its grounding in American graphic vernacular and persuasive communication.

name: Calibre
classification_notes: Geometric neo-grotesque in the rationalist tradition. Draws directly from Aldo Novarese's Recta (Nebiolo, late 1950s), refining its logic without its original optical over-corrections. Shares a fundamental geometric skeleton with its sister typeface Metric, but applies sharper, more rationalist letterform finishes where Metric opts for humanist softness. Classified as Modern Lineal / Neo-grotesque.
summary: A geometric neo-grotesque by Kris Sowersby that channels the rationalist precision of Aldo Novarese's Recta, sharpened into a crisp, contemporary workhorse available in seven weights.
description: Designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2011, Calibre takes the rationalist logic of Nebiolo's late-1950s Recta as its starting point, correcting that typeface's awkward branching and optical over-corrections into something leaner and more precise. It shares an underlying geometric framework with its sister face Metric but diverges at the letterform details, landing firmly in the rationalist camp of the neo-grotesque tradition. Running from Thin to Black with matching italics across all seven weights, it is a thorough workhorse equally at home in editorial, UI and corporate settings.
foundry_blurb: Calibre is a geometric neo-grotesque drawing from the rationalist tradition of Aldo Novarese's Recta, a rarely seen late-1950s typeface produced by a team at the now-defunct Nebiolo foundry. Where Recta was held back by over-correction and awkward branching, Calibre refines that underlying logic into something crisp and contemporary. It shares a fundamental geometry with its sister typeface Metric but applies letterforms from a distinct rationalist tradition, making the two complementary but fully independent families.

name: Die Grotesk
classification_notes: Modern neo-grotesque drawn in deliberate dialogue with Helvetica and Neue Haas Grotesk; informed by original metal specimens and Massimo Vignelli's tight-spacing approach to lockups and logotypes. Klim's first retail variable font, with continuous weight (100–900) and optical size (6–42pt) axes. Four discrete optical-size cuts (A through D) replace conventional tracking adjustments across body and display use.
summary: Klim's first retail variable font – a neo-grotesque in direct dialogue with Helvetica, built across four optical-size cuts and eight weights in roman and italic.
description: Designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2025, Die Grotesk draws from original metal specimens of Neue Haas Grotesk and the rigour of modernist masters to engage Helvetica's legacy rather than sidestep it. Four optical-size subfamilies (A through D) provide purposeful spacing calibrated from dense body copy to tight display lockups, replacing crude tracking adjustments with precision engineered into the letterforms. A continuous weight axis (100–900) and optical size axis (6–42pt) give designers exacting control over typographic texture at every scale.
foundry_blurb: Shaped in the long shadow of Helvetica, Die Grotesk draws from the study of original metal cuts and the rigour of modernist masters. Its variable axes give precise control of weight and letter spacing across every size, built to handle the tension between reverence for an iconic grotesk tradition and the practical demands of contemporary design. Engineered with manual VTT hinting and 22,165 manual kerning pairs per style, it meets the exacting standards Klim applies to every retail release.

name: Domaine Display
classification_notes: Modern Transitional/Latin. High contrast, sharp display cut with gently bracketed triangular serifs and distinctive hooked terminals. Klim classifies it as Modern: Transitional/Latin. The italics draw on early 20th-century French precendents (Deberny & Peignot's Labeurs Ordinaires Série) rather than strict historical revival forms.
summary: A sharp, high-contrast display serif by Kris Sowersby that fuses French and British typographic traditions into a contemporary voice, spanning six weights with matching italics.
description: Domaine Display was released in 2013 and draws on early 20th-century French and British serif traditions. Its gently bracketed triangular serifs, hooked terminals and calm horizontal head serifs give it a cool, precise elegance suited to editorial headlines and brand identities. The italics take their cue from Deberny & Peignot's Labeurs Ordinaires Série, adding a scholarly warmth to the roman's crispness. The family extends to Display Narrow, Display Condensed and a companion Text cut for body settings, making it a complete display system.
foundry_blurb: Klim describes Domaine Display as a sharp, elegant serif that blends traditional French and British genres into a contemporary aesthetic – characterised by gently bracketed triangular serifs, distinctive hooked terminals and italics inspired by Deberny & Peignot's Labeurs Ordinaires Série. It is part of a broader Domaine system comprising Display, Narrow, Condensed and Text cuts totalling 46 styles.

name: Domaine Display Condensed
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Modern: Transitional/Latin; the condensed display cut of Domaine, with bracketed triangular serifs, hooked terminals and italics drawn from Deberny & Peignot's Labeurs Ordinaires Série.
summary: A condensed display serif holding Domaine's triangular serifs and hooked terminals at tight measures for fashion and editorial mastheads.
description: A sharp condensed display serif by Kris Sowersby, the tightest cut in the Domaine Display system, with bracketed triangular serifs, hooked terminals and italics inspired by Deberny & Peignot's Labeurs Ordinaires Série. Twelve styles run from Regular to Black with matching italics, made to keep their elegance when set in narrow columns or stacked over images. Frequently paired with Domaine Text and Söhne in fashion, wine and editorial branding.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Domaine Display Condensed as Modern: Transitional/Latin, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2013. They describe Domaine as a sharp serif blending French and British genres, with bracketed triangular serifs and hooked terminals, and italics drawn from Deberny & Peignot's Labeurs Ordinaires Série. This is the condensed display cut within the wider Domaine system.

name: Domaine Display Narrow
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Modern: Transitional/Latin; the narrow display cut between the standard Display and the Condensed, sharing Domaine's triangular serifs, hooked terminals and Deberny & Peignot italics.
summary: A narrow display serif sitting between Domaine Display and Domaine Display Condensed, made for tight headlines that keep their elegance.
description: A narrow display serif by Kris Sowersby, the middle width within the Domaine Display system, with bracketed triangular serifs, hooked terminals and italics inspired by Deberny & Peignot's Labeurs Ordinaires Série. Twelve styles run from Regular to Black with matching italics, more economical than Domaine Display itself but less compressed than Domaine Display Condensed. A natural fit for fashion, wine and editorial mastheads where the columns are tight but the brand still wants air.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Domaine Display Narrow as Modern: Transitional/Latin, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2013. They describe Domaine as a sharp serif blending French and British genres, with bracketed triangular serifs and hooked terminals, and italics drawn from Deberny & Peignot's Labeurs Ordinaires Série. This cut is the narrow display width within the Domaine system.

name: Domaine Sans
classification_notes: Lineal grotesque with deliberate stroke contrast — an exploration of the Breite Grotesk subgenre. Shares the skeleton of Domaine (the Klim serif family) per Martin Majoor's one-form principle. Terminals taper to hairlines rather than flaring. Italic draws on mid-century lettering artist Mortimer Leach and features optional swash capitals for every uppercase letter. Three optical subfamilies: Fine (60pt+), Display (headlines), Text (sustained reading).
summary: A high-contrast grotesque in three optical subfamilies, grown from the Domaine skeleton and the neglected tradition of Breite Grotesk.
description: Domaine Sans began as an experiment: stripping the serifs from Domaine Text Light to reveal the skeleton beneath, then following that logic into the under-exploited genre of sans serifs with visible stroke contrast. Sowersby drew on Optima, Britannic (1924), Breite Grotesk and the Art Deco lettering from Napier's 1931 earthquake rebuilding, using Martin Majoor's one-form principle to hold the three optical subfamilies together. Fine is for use above 60pt; Display handles headlines; Text is built for extended reading — 42 styles in total, each with italics featuring optional swash capitals across every uppercase letter.
foundry_blurb: Domaine explored the neglected Latin serif genre; Domaine Sans follows into another unpopular territory: sans serifs with contrast. The family spans three optical subfamilies — Fine, Display and Text — covering up to eight weights each with corresponding italics and swash alternate capitals, built with manual VTT hinting and extensive kerning. Awarded TDC² Judge's Choice (2015) and entered into the Cooper Hewitt permanent collection (2016).

name: Domaine Sans Display
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Lineal: Grotesque, High Contrast; the display cut of Domaine Sans, an exploration of contrast in sans serifs alongside Domaine's earlier work in the Latin serif genre.
summary: A high-contrast display sans by Kris Sowersby that explores contrast in sanserifs, made for fashion and editorial display.
description: A high-contrast display sans by Kris Sowersby, sitting at the largest size in the Domaine Sans system. Sixteen styles run from Thin to Black with matching italics, with swashes and old-style or lining numerals available through OpenType. Klim describe Domaine Sans as an exploration of an unpopular genre, sans serifs with contrast, and at display sizes the stress and modulation read clearly, which is why fashion and editorial brands such as Vanity Fair's Hollywood issue have reached for it.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Domaine Sans Display as Lineal: Grotesque, High Contrast, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2014. They describe Domaine Sans as an exploration of an unpopular genre, sans serifs with contrast, following Domaine's earlier exploration of the Latin serif genre.

name: Domaine Sans Fine
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Lineal: Grotesque, High Contrast; the finest optical cut of Domaine Sans, with the sharpest contrast, sharing the family's exploration of contrasted sans serifs.
summary: The sharpest optical cut of Domaine Sans, with the highest contrast for large-scale luxury and editorial display.
description: The Fine optical size of Domaine Sans by Kris Sowersby, drawn for the largest display sizes where the family's contrast can read at its sharpest. Sixteen styles run from Thin to Black with matching italics. Specimens for Domaine Sans were added to the Cooper Hewitt Collection in 2016, and the Fine cut tends to appear in luxury, fashion and high-end editorial work where the brief calls for the punch of a Didone but in a sans frame.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Domaine Sans Fine as Lineal: Grotesque, High Contrast, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2014. They describe Domaine Sans as an exploration of sans serifs with contrast, following Domaine's earlier exploration of the Latin serif genre. Fine is the highest-contrast optical size in the system.

name: Domaine Sans Text
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Lineal: Grotesque, High Contrast; the text optical size of Domaine Sans, sharing the family's exploration of sans serifs with contrast and adding small caps for setting body copy.
summary: The text cut of Domaine Sans, with reduced contrast and small caps for body copy that still carries the family's editorial voice.
description: The Text optical size of Domaine Sans by Kris Sowersby, with the family's contrast tempered for body sizes and small caps added for editorial setting. Ten styles span Light to Black with matching italics, alongside small caps, all small caps, tabular figures and superiors. Reads with the warmth and authority of a serif text face while staying inside the sans genre, which is why it pairs neatly with Domaine Display, Domaine Text and Tiempos Text in editorial systems.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Domaine Sans Text as Lineal: Grotesque, High Contrast, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2014. They describe Domaine Sans as an exploration of sans serifs with contrast, following Domaine's earlier exploration of the Latin serif genre. Text is the optical size tuned for body copy.

name: Domaine Text
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Modern: Transitional/Latin; the text cut of Domaine, with the family's bracketed triangular serifs, hooked terminals and Deberny & Peignot italics, with small caps and figure sets for editorial body copy.
summary: The text optical size of Domaine, tuned for body copy with small caps and figure sets while keeping the family's sharpness.
description: The Text optical size of Domaine by Kris Sowersby, where the family's bracketed triangular serifs and hooked terminals are recut for body sizes. Ten styles run Light to Black with matching italics drawn from Deberny & Peignot's Labeurs Ordinaires Série, alongside small caps, all small caps and tabular figures. Pairs neatly with Domaine Display and Domaine Display Narrow in editorial, wine and luxury identities where you want the same voice from masthead to running text.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Domaine Text as Modern: Transitional/Latin, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2008. They describe Domaine as a sharp serif blending French and British genres, with bracketed triangular serifs and hooked terminals, and italics inspired by Deberny & Peignot's Labeurs Ordinaires Série. Text is the optical size cut for body copy.

name: Epicene Display
classification_notes: Baroque Old-Style drawing from 18th-century Dutch masters Jacques-François Rosart (1714–1777) and Johann Michael Fleischmann (1707–1768); not a revival but a modernisation, synthesising Rosart's exaggerated geometric capitals with Fleischmann's ink-pooled, small-text sensibility; signature scalloped serifs combine the smooth inner curve from Rosart with the sharp outer scallop from Fleischmann, adapted to function across the full character set at both body and display sizes; available as two optical cuts – Display and Text – each with five weights and matching italics.
summary: A Baroque Old-Style serif in two optical cuts, synthesising the work of 18th-century Dutch masters Rosart and Fleischmann, with the cultural argument baked into its name: typefaces carry no gender.
description: Released in September 2021, Epicene exists as Display and Text cuts, each offering five weights with matching italics. Kris Sowersby drew from Rosart's exaggerated geometric capitals and Fleischmann's ink-dense, small-text italics, arriving at a distinctive scalloped serif that sits at the crossing of both designers' sensibilities and reads with equal conviction at headline and body sizes. The name comes from Susan Sontag's "Notes on Camp" – epicene meaning lacking gender distinction – a deliberate pushback against the long-held coding of ornamental type as feminine and functional forms as masculine.
foundry_blurb: Epicene Text and Display are Baroque typefaces inspired by 18th-century maestros J-F. Rosart and J.M. Fleischmann. Exaggerated details add rigour at small sizes and vigour at large sizes. The collection's cultural statement: typefaces have no gender.

name: Epicene Text
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Baroque Old-Style; the text counterpart to Epicene Display, drawing on Rosart and Fleischmann with details tuned to add rigour at small sizes.
summary: A Baroque text serif drawn from Rosart and Fleischmann, tuned with quieter detail for body copy in books and editorial.
description: A Baroque text serif by Kris Sowersby and the body-copy companion to Epicene Display, rooted in the same 18th century work of Rosart and Fleischmann. Five roman weights from Light to Black come with matching italics, with details settled down so the page reads steady at book and magazine sizes. Reaches for a literary register where Tiempos Text would feel too neutral and a Garalde revival would feel too quiet.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Epicene Text as a Baroque Old-Style, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2021. They pair it with Epicene Display in a single Baroque family inspired by J-F. Rosart and J.M. Fleischmann, with details tuned to add rigour at small sizes.

name: Family
classification_notes: Oldstyle serif revival of Clearface (ATF, 1907, Morris Fuller Benton and Linn Boyd Benton). Retains Clearface's elliptical terminals, open single-storey 'g', sloped 'e' crossbar and strong thick-thin contrast. Serifs are thin slabs on thick strokes, bracketed on thin strokes – a structural trait inherited from the original. Variable font weight axis 300–900.
summary: Kris Sowersby's 2023 revival of Clearface, keeping the 1907 ATF original's elliptical terminals and informal warmth while reworking anything that didn't survive the digital transition cleanly.
description: Family takes Morris Fuller Benton's 1907 Clearface as its source, preserving the easy-going curves, elliptical terminals and open single-storey 'g' that give the original its character. Sowersby keeps deliberate idiosyncrasies – the sloped 'e' crossbar, the consistent f and j overhang – while quietly resolving the strokes on A, V and W that never translated well into digital. Six weights with matching italics and a variable font axis make it practical across text and display sizes.
foundry_blurb: Family is an everyday typeface based on Clearface, originally designed by father and son Morris Fuller and Linn Boyd Benton. It keeps Clearface's easy-going curves and idiosyncrasies while updating it for modern use.

name: Feijoa
classification_notes: Garalde (Aldine) oldstyle serif, classified by Klim as Modern: Garalde/Oldstyle. Deliberately curvaceous letterforms with all sharp angles resolved into gentle curves. Four styles spanning a Display cut (headline-optimised, 16pt and above) and text weights in Medium and Bold with accompanying italic. Klim's inaugural typeface.
summary: Klim's debut release: a warm Garalde serif built on the principle that a straight line is a dead line, with deliberately curvaceous letterforms across a text range and a headline-specific Display cut.
description: Feijoa was the first typeface issued by Klim Type Foundry, released in 2007. Designed by Kris Sowersby, it takes a Garalde oldstyle structure and resolves every sharp angle into a gentle curve, humanising the letterforms without undermining their authority at text sizes. The family runs to four styles spanning a text range (Medium and Bold) and a Display cut drawn for 16pt and above, with fanciful ligatures inspired by Zuzana Licko's Mrs Eaves adding an extra layer of typographic warmth.
foundry_blurb: Feijoa is built on the idea that a straight line is a dead line. The result is warm, curvaceous letterforms that sidestep the sharp angles which can harm digital typefaces, giving the overall impression a distinctly human quality. The core family — Medium, Italic and Bold — suits book typography and extended reading; the Display weight is drawn specifically for headlines at 16pt and above. All styles include fanciful ligatures and a suite of OpenType features including small caps, multiple stylistic sets and contextual alternates.

name: Financier Display
classification_notes: High-contrast serif commissioned for the Financial Times. Display cut draws from Eric Gill's Perpetua – stately caps, sharp joins, flat unbracketed serifs without ink traps. Italics reconcile mechanical sloped Romans with calligraphic tradition. Numerals receive special treatment reflecting Gill's flat-top 3s and three-quarter-height 2s, suited to data-heavy editorial contexts. A companion Text cut (separate retail product) draws more from Gill's Solus and Joanna for body-copy use.
summary: A high-contrast editorial serif drawn for the Financial Times in 2014, Financier Display takes its authority from Eric Gill's Perpetua across six weights from Light to Black.
description: Designed by Kris Sowersby and commissioned for the Financial Times' 2014 redesign, Financier Display draws its formal character from Eric Gill's Perpetua: sharp joins, flat unbracketed serifs and carefully crafted numerals that hold up in data-heavy layouts. Six weights spanning Light to Black, each with a matching italic, give it genuine range across headlines, pull quotes and financial tables. A variable font covering the full 300–900 weight axis ships with the full family purchase.
foundry_blurb: Klim describes Financier as an elegant, authoritative serif with an undeniable British heritage. The Display cut takes its stately quality from Perpetua, while the companion Text cut applies pragmatic detailing drawn from Solus and Joanna. The italics are designed to reconcile mechanical sloped Romans with traditional calligraphic forms, creating a formal typographic atmosphere that never feels dry.

name: Financier Text
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Modern: Transitional/Slab Serif; the text counterpart drawn for the 2014 Financial Times redesign, with pragmatic detailing taken from Solus and Joanna in the Gill lineage.
summary: A transitional text serif with slab leanings, drawn from Gill's Solus and Joanna for the 2014 Financial Times redesign.
description: A transitional text serif by Kris Sowersby, the body-copy companion to Financier Display drawn for the 2014 Financial Times redesign. Pragmatic detailing comes from Eric Gill's Solus and Joanna, giving it a slab leaning that holds shape on broadsheets and on narrow mobile screens. Four weights from Regular to Black across eight styles plus variable roman and italic axes carry features, news and longform across the FT's wider editorial system.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Financier Text as Modern: Transitional/Slab Serif, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2016. They describe it as the text counterpart to Financier Display, drawn for the 2014 Financial Times redesign, with pragmatic detailing taken from Solus and Joanna in Eric Gill's lineage.

name: Founders Grotesk
classification_notes: Modern grotesque drawing on Millar & Richard's 1912 Grotesque series and H.W. Caslon's Doric series (1919), with spacing influenced by Helvetica Halbfett headline cuts from the late 1950s. Serpentine S, narrow apertures on C and G, and selective historical letterform choices give it warmth uncommon in contemporary grotesques.
summary: A contemporary grotesque synthesising early 20th-century British foundry specimens – Millar & Richard and H.W. Caslon's Doric – into a large, versatile collection spanning core, Text, Condensed, X-Condensed and Mono variants.
description: Designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2010, Founders Grotesk draws from Millar & Richard's 1912 Grotesque series and H.W. Caslon's Doric, coupling their serpentine curves and narrow apertures with the close spacing of Helvetica Halbfett headline cuts. The collection spans five sub-families covering tight display work down to small-body legibility, with the Text variant developed separately after the headline original proved too tight at reading sizes. Condensed and X-Condensed cuts draw on Miller & Richard's Sans-Serif No.5 for square inner counters contrasted against warm outer curves.
foundry_blurb: Klim describe Founders Grotesk as a gentle amalgamation of several early grotesques rather than a strict revival, combining rudimentary geometry and serpentine curves from Millar & Richard's Grotesque series with selected details from H.W. Caslon's Doric, spaced to match the close-set Helvetica Halbfett headline metal cuts of the late 1950s.

name: Founders Grotesk Condensed
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Modern: Lineal/Grotesque; the condensed cut of Founders Grotesk, an amalgamation of Miller & Richard's early 20th century Grotesque series, H. W. Caslon's Doric and Helvetica's Halbfett headline cuts.
summary: A condensed grotesque drawn from Miller & Richard, Caslon Doric and Helvetica headline cuts, built for tight headlines and posters.
description: The condensed cut of Founders Grotesk, by Kris Sowersby, pulling rudimentary geometry and serpentine curves from Miller & Richard's early 20th century Grotesque series, further details from H. W. Caslon's Doric series, and tight spacing strategies from Helvetica's Halbfett headline-sized metal cuts of the late 1950s. Five weights from Light to Bold give posters, mastheads and packaging a confident, editorial-feeling condensed sans without the rigidity of a strict revival. Sits within the wider Founders Grotesk system alongside the standard, Text, X-Condensed and Mono cuts.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Founders Grotesk Condensed as Modern: Lineal/Grotesque, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2011. They describe Founders Grotesk as a contemporary amalgamation of classic grotesks, drawing on Miller & Richard's Grotesque series, H. W. Caslon's Doric and the tight spacing of Helvetica's Halbfett headline cuts from the late 1950s.

name: Founders Grotesk Mono
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Modern: Lineal/Grotesque Monospaced; the monospaced cut of Founders Grotesk, sharing the family's roots in Miller & Richard's Grotesque series, Caslon's Doric and Helvetica's Halbfett headline cuts.
summary: A grotesque monospace inside the Founders Grotesk system, fit for code, editorial detail and brand pairings.
description: The monospaced cut of Founders Grotesk, by Kris Sowersby, sharing the lineage of Miller & Richard's Grotesque series, H. W. Caslon's Doric and Helvetica's Halbfett headline cuts. Five weights from Light to Bold sit alongside the parent Founders Grotesk, Text, Condensed and X-Condensed cuts, with a slashed zero, fractions and capital forms in the OpenType set. Used widely in editorial captions, code blocks and brand systems where the mono needs to hold a conversation with a wider grotesque family.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Founders Grotesk Mono as Modern: Lineal/Grotesque Monospaced, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2014. They describe the parent Founders Grotesk as a contemporary amalgamation of classic grotesks drawing on Miller & Richard's Grotesque series, Caslon's Doric and Helvetica's Halbfett, with the Mono extending those forms onto a fixed pitch.

name: Founders Grotesk Text
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Modern: Lineal/Grotesque; the text-sized cut of Founders Grotesk, with the same lineage as the wider family but tuned for body copy.
summary: The text cut of Founders Grotesk, with five weights and italics tuned for body copy in editorial and brand systems.
description: The text cut of Founders Grotesk, by Kris Sowersby, redrawn from the parent grotesque so it holds shape at body sizes. Five weights from Light to Bold across ten styles include true italics, with the same lineage of Miller & Richard's Grotesque series, Caslon's Doric and Helvetica's Halbfett headline cuts. Used as the workhorse text companion in brand and editorial systems where Founders Grotesk runs the headlines, with Condensed, X-Condensed and Mono extending the family.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Founders Grotesk Text as Modern: Lineal/Grotesque, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2013. They describe Founders Grotesk as a contemporary amalgamation of classic grotesks drawing on Miller & Richard's Grotesque series, H. W. Caslon's Doric and Helvetica's Halbfett headline cuts, with the Text cut tuned for body copy.

name: Founders Grotesk X-Condensed
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Modern: Lineal/Grotesque; the extra-condensed cut of Founders Grotesk, sharing the family's roots in Miller & Richard's Grotesque series, Caslon's Doric and Helvetica's Halbfett.
summary: An extra-condensed grotesque inside the Founders Grotesk system, drawn for posters, mastheads and tight vertical headlines.
description: The extra-condensed cut of Founders Grotesk, by Kris Sowersby, narrower again than the Condensed and tuned for posters, mastheads and stacked headlines. Five weights from Light to Bold sit beside the standard Founders Grotesk, Text, Condensed and Mono cuts, sharing the same lineage of Miller & Richard's Grotesque series, Caslon's Doric and Helvetica's Halbfett headline metal cuts. The cut culture studios reach for when a grotesque has to set a long word in a short column without thinning the weight.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Founders Grotesk X-Condensed as Modern: Lineal/Grotesque, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2011. They describe Founders Grotesk as a contemporary amalgamation of classic grotesks drawing on Miller & Richard's Grotesque series, H. W. Caslon's Doric and Helvetica's Halbfett headline cuts, with the X-Condensed cut taking those forms to an extra-narrow proportion.

name: Geograph
classification_notes: Contemporary geometric sans-serif that calibrates between the idealism of Futura and the practicality of Super Grotesk. Commissioned for National Geographic's 2016 rebrand to replace Verlag and Neue Haas Grotesk across print, digital and broadcast; publicly released 2019. Available as a variable font (wght axis 200–900) with full family purchase. Three stylistic sets: Futura-style alternates for G, S, a, e, g, j, s, t, u (ss01); crossed W (ss02); blunt stroke alternates for A, M, N, V, W and numerals (ss03). The blunt alternate set effectively delivers an "Edit" register within a single font, echoing a bespoke variant made for the original National Geographic commission.
summary: A geometric sans-serif commissioned for National Geographic that mediates between Futura's idealism and Super Grotesk's practicality, with six weights, matching italics, and three stylistic sets for fine-grained tonal control.
description: Geograph was commissioned by National Geographic in 2016 to replace Verlag and Neue Haas Grotesk across print, digital and broadcast, then publicly released by Klim in 2019. Kris Sowersby drew from Futura's idealistic geometry and Super Grotesk's functional range, arriving at a face that performs equally at display and editorial scale. Three stylistic sets – Futura-style alternates, a crossed W, and blunt stroke endings – give designers unusual control over the typeface's tone, from warm and geometric to sharp and contemporary.
foundry_blurb: Geograph is a contemporary geometric sans-serif originally designed for National Geographic. Klim describe it as drawing on the idealism of Futura and the pragmatism of Super Grotesk, with a suite of alternate letterforms that enable flexible typographic textures. It comes in six weights each with a matching italic, plus a variable font with full family purchase.

name: Heldane Display
classification_notes: Third-generation garalde/oldstyle, synthesising Renaissance punchcutting traditions from van den Keere, Garamont, Granjon and de Colines. High contrast with sharp, tense serifs and dense lowercase. Optimised for display sizes; companion Heldane Text handles body copy. Classified Garalde/Oldstyle.
summary: A sharply drawn garalde display serif over a decade in the making, synthesising van den Keere, Garamont, Granjon and de Colines into a unified face with genuine historical depth.
description: Designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2018, Heldane Display draws its lowercase character from Hendrik van den Keere's dense aesthetic, its capital forms from Simon de Colines, and its numerals from Robert Granjon. Optimised for large sizes, it pairs with Heldane Text for body setting – together forming a complete editorial system. The family took over a decade to develop and received recognition from the Type Directors Club, Tokyo TDC and Graphis Typography.
foundry_blurb: A contemporary serif inspired by the renaissance work of Hendrik van den Keere, Claude Garamont, Robert Granjon and Simon de Colines, drawing the strongest details from each source rather than copying any single model and synthesising them into a cohesive whole.

name: Heldane Text
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Classical: Garalde/Oldstyle; a contemporary serif drawing on Hendrik van den Keere, Claude Garamont, Robert Granjon and Simon de Colines, with old-style numerals, small caps and a full italic swash programme tuned for body text.
summary: A contemporary garalde text serif blending Garamont, Granjon, van den Keere and de Colines, sturdy enough to carry long-form body copy.
description: A garalde text serif by Kris Sowersby drawn from the renaissance work of Hendrik van den Keere, Claude Garamont, Robert Granjon and Simon de Colines, refined through digital drawing for present-day setting. Six styles run Regular, Medium and Bold with italics, plus small caps, old-style and tabular numerals, and a swash programme inherited from the Display cut. The Text size in the Heldane system, paired naturally with Heldane Display for headlines.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Heldane Text as Classical: Garalde/Oldstyle, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2018. They describe Heldane as a contemporary serif inspired by the renaissance works of Hendrik van den Keere, Claude Garamont, Robert Granjon and Simon de Colines, amalgamating their best details rather than emulating any single typeface.

name: Karbon
classification_notes: Open geometric sans-serif in the modernist tradition; Klim classifies it as "Modern: Lineal/Geometric". The Karbon Slab Stencil sub-family is classified "Modern: Mechanistic/Stencil". Low contrast, geometric construction, open apertures with a spartan, reductive finish.
summary: An open geometric sans-serif channelling Futura's reductionist logic through Gill's proportions, with a clean spartan finish across seven weights.
description: Designed by Kris Sowersby in 2009, Karbon draws on three modernist references: Renner's Futura for its reductionist concept, Eric Gill's sans for its proportions, and Jan Tschichold's Uhertype as a further touchpoint. Seven weights with italics hold a contemporary restraint that works across both display and text sizes. The Slab Stencil extension applies the same sparse logic to an industrial stencil form, with deliberate breaks running through the letterforms.
foundry_blurb: Klim describes Karbon as an open geometric sans-serif with a contemporary spartan finish – a take on Paul Renner's Futura concept filtered through the proportions of Eric Gill's sans, with a nod to Jan Tschichold's Uhertype. The Slab Stencil variant extends the family's spare linework into slab-serif territory, with a programme of breaks referencing industrial stencilled letterforms.

name: Karbon Slab Stencil
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Modern: Mechanistic/Stencil; extends Karbon's spartan geometric linework into slab-serif territory, with a logical programme of breaks referencing the industrial heritage of stencilled letterforms.
summary: Karbon's geometric skeleton pushed into slab-serif territory with stencilled breaks, fit for industrial and utility-flavoured display work.
description: A stencil slab by Kris Sowersby that takes the spartan geometry of Karbon and adds slab serifs plus a logical pattern of breaks, citing the industrial heritage of stencilled letterforms. Two styles only, Regular and Bold, with no italic. Sits as a display companion to Karbon proper, useful for posters, packaging and signage that wants a mechanical, slightly utilitarian voice.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Karbon Slab Stencil as Modern: Mechanistic/Stencil, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2009. They describe it as an extension of Karbon's spartan linework into slab-serif territory, with a logical programme of breaks referencing the industrial heritage of stencilled letterforms.

name: Maelstrom
classification_notes: Inverts conventional stroke contrast: horizontals are heavy, verticals taper to hairlines. Draws directly from 19th-century reversed-stress wood type – Caslon Italian (1821), Miller & Richard French Antique (c. 1865), Debow's Italian (c. 1837). Available in a single Bold weight only, making it a pure display face. The companion Maelstrom Sans (2019) removes the slabs but keeps the reversed-stress logic, replacing slab terminations with the heavy-horizontal, spindly-diagonal contrast of a reversed grotesque. Both sit firmly in the display category with no text weights.
summary: A single-weight reversed-stress slab serif from Kris Sowersby, rooted in 19th-century Italian wood type, with hairline verticals and massive horizontals that create a luminous, almost electric texture at display sizes.
description: Maelstrom inverts the conventional hierarchy of stroke weight: its horizontals carry the mass while verticals taper to near-invisible hairlines, with side bearings of just 3 UPM producing those characteristic narrow strips of light through the black letterform. Released in 2014, it draws on historical models including Caslon Italian and Miller & Richard's French Antique, reinterpreted with Sowersby's exacting craft and slight serif bracketing to soften an otherwise extreme contrast. A companion, Maelstrom Sans (2019), strips the slabs entirely, pushing the perverse logic further with heavy horizontals and fragile diagonal strokes.
foundry_blurb: Maelstrom and Maelstrom Sans are reversed-stress typefaces – perpetual typographic outsiders, never mainstream yet never forgotten. Maelstrom's razor-thin spacing forms narrow strips of light sparkling through the black mass, while Maelstrom Sans combines heavy horizontals and spindly diagonals for a deliberately fragile effect. Their perverse quality is precisely their defining strength.

name: Maelstrom Sans
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as a Reversed-Stress Sans Serif; an uneasy mix of heavy horizontals and spindly diagonals that feels fragile, like it could splinter at any moment. Sits in the Maelstrom collection alongside the slab-serif Maelstrom.
summary: A single-weight reversed-stress display sans of heavy horizontals and spindly diagonals, made for posters and identity rather than text.
description: A reversed-stress display sans by Kris Sowersby that flips weight onto the horizontals and starves the diagonals, giving it a fragile, almost splintering quality. Released as a single Bold cut, no italic, no other widths. Sits in the Maelstrom collection alongside the slab-serif Maelstrom and belongs to the genre Klim describe as a perpetual typographic outsider, never fashionable yet never abandoned.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Maelstrom Sans as a Reversed-Stress Sans Serif, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2019. They describe Maelstrom and Maelstrom Sans as deliberately perverse reversed-stress typefaces, with Maelstrom Sans's uneasy mix of heavy horizontals and spindly diagonals making it feel fragile, like it could splinter at any moment.

name: Martina Plantijn
classification_notes: Oldstyle serif revival rooted in Frank Hinman Pierpont's Plantin (1913), which itself drew from Robert Granjon's Gros Cicero (1569) and research at the Plantin-Moretus Museum in Antwerp. Variable weight axis spanning 300–900. Distinctive blunt-leg 'k' (a Pierpont signature) carried through related letterforms including R, K, Q and the italic f, j, z. Corner apexes clipped throughout for an analogue quality. Italic returns to Renaissance punch-cutters rather than the weaker British-modern influence of the original Plantin italic.
summary: Kris Sowersby's third engagement with Plantin — a rigorous revival that goes back to 16th-century sources at the Plantin-Moretus Museum, tightening the roman's proportions and giving the italic the Renaissance energy the original always lacked.
description: Martina Plantijn takes Frank Hinman Pierpont's 1913 text workhorse back to its primary sources: Robert Granjon's Gros Cicero (1569) and the specimens held at the Plantin-Moretus Museum in Antwerp. The roman corrects Plantin's overly wide proportions and uncertain drawing; the italic sheds its weak British-modern influence for something more compact and energetic, closer to the renaissance punch-cutters Pierpont was originally studying. The name honours Martina Plantin (1541–1599), daughter of printer Christophe Plantin, who ran the family printing business from 1610 to 1614.
foundry_blurb: Klim describes Martina Plantijn as a better Plantin — informed by the workhorse qualities of Pierpont's typeface, expanded through first-hand research into 16th-century type at the Plantin-Moretus Museum in Antwerp, with decisive digital updates made across both the roman and italic cuts.

name: Metric
classification_notes: Geometric humanist sans serif with monoline construction and optically corrected letterforms. Inspired by West Berlin street sign lettering, which Sowersby traces to a template derived from Jakob Erbar's Erbar typeface. Shares core geometry with Calibre but takes distinct decisions on key letterforms: Metric uses an oval 'a' bowl and severe vertical terminal cuts where Calibre applies neo-grotesque alternates drawn from Novarese's Recta. The result sits between pure geometric sans and humanist warmth.
summary: A geometric humanist sans serif drawn from West Berlin street sign lettering, pairing monoline rationality with careful optical correction across seven weights and matching italics.
description: Metric was released in 2011 by Kris Sowersby, its design rooted in the elegant lettering he encountered on West Berlin street signs – a tradition traced to Jakob Erbar's early geometric sans. The typeface shares a structural geometry with its sibling Calibre but diverges in key letterform decisions, applying optical corrections to produce something rational without the coldness of strict geometric construction. Seven weights from Thin to Black, each with a matching italic, give it genuine range across text and display work.
foundry_blurb: Metric is a geometric humanist sans serif inspired by the lettering found on West Berlin street signs. Its monoline construction feels rational and unpretentious, with optical corrections applied throughout to temper the engineer's geometry with typographic judgement. Developed alongside Calibre, the two families share a common structure but take different paths at key letterforms.

name: Mānuka
classification_notes: Klim classifies Mānuka as Lineal: Grotesque. Designed specifically for display and large-scale use, the family is compressed throughout with tight spacing, closed apertures and sharp joins derived from an 1860s German wood-type specimen by Will & Schumacher, Mannheim. The sharp joins in strokes (d, h, n, m, u) are highly unusual for sans-serif construction and distinguish it clearly from conventional grotesques. Part of a three-family collection alongside Mānuka Condensed (more compressed) and Mānuka Slab (slab-serif variant drawn from the same specimen's slab series, Nº 264–282).
summary: A compressed display grotesque by Kris Sowersby, distilled from an 1860s German wood-type specimen and built for headline use across seven weights.
description: Mānuka takes its starting point from a numbered wood-type specimen by Will & Schumacher, Mannheim, circa 1860s, translating the original's mechanical compression and unusually sharp stroke joins into a contemporary display grotesque. Released in 2021, it spans seven weights from Thin to Ultra and sits alongside Mānuka Condensed and Mānuka Slab as part of a broader collection. Tight spacing, closed apertures and carefully preserved eccentric details – an elegant R kick, a serpentine g link, an elongated r terminal – give it a distinctive, angular texture uncommon in grotesque revival work.
foundry_blurb: Klim describes Mānuka as "new growth from old wood" – a collection of compressed fonts for large sizes that grafts a contemporary antipodean aesthetic onto 19th-century German root-stock. Deviant details borrowed from Teutonic timber type produce tight spacing, closed apertures and sharp joins that create what they call a compelling texture, "like sunlight sparkling through a forest canopy."

name: Mānuka Condensed
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Lineal: Grotesque; a collection of compressed fonts for large sizes, with deviant details pilfered from Teutonic timber type, grafting a contemporary antipodean aesthetic onto 19th century German root-stock.
summary: A compressed grotesque cut from Teutonic wood-type roots, running Thin to Ultra for posters, packaging and bold display lockups.
description: A compressed display grotesque by Kris Sowersby with sharp joins, closed apertures and tight spacing, pulling deviant details from 19th century Teutonic timber type. Seven upright weights run from Thin to Ultra, no italics. Sits in the Mānuka collection alongside Mānuka Slab, and works hardest at very large sizes where the compressed texture reads, in Klim's words, like sunlight sparkling through a forest canopy.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Mānuka Condensed as Lineal: Grotesque, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2021. They describe Mānuka as new growth from old wood, a collection of compressed fonts for large sizes, grafting a contemporary antipodean aesthetic onto 19th century German timber-type root-stock.

name: Mānuka Slab
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Modern: Slab-Serif; the slab cut of the Mānuka collection, sharing compressed proportions and Teutonic timber-type details with Mānuka Condensed.
summary: The slab partner to Mānuka Condensed, compressed and rooted in Teutonic timber type, running Thin to Ultra for display work.
description: A compressed slab by Kris Sowersby that takes Mānuka's antipodean reading of 19th century Teutonic timber type and adds slab serifs. Seven upright weights run from Thin to Ultra with stylistic alternates for a and R, no italics. Pairs naturally with Mānuka Condensed inside the same collection, and earns its keep on posters, packaging and editorial display where the texture needs to feel hand-cut rather than digital.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Mānuka Slab as Modern: Slab-Serif, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2021. They describe Mānuka as new growth from old wood, a collection of compressed fonts for large sizes, with deviant details pilfered from Teutonic timber type and grafted onto a contemporary antipodean aesthetic.

name: National
classification_notes: Revival of 19th-century English and American grotesques, drawn as a stylistic counterpoint to Helvetica. Features looser spacing, unambiguous forms, old-style figures as default, angled Akzidenz-era terminals, and a true italic rather than an oblique. Single width, 18 styles across 9 weights.
summary: A workmanlike grotesque rooted in 19th-century English and American type, drawn as a deliberate counterpoint to Helvetica with looser spacing, unambiguous forms and a true italic.
description: Released in 2007 and a TDC Judge's Choice winner the following year, National draws its character from the pre-Akzidenz grotesque tradition – giving it a quieter, more considered presence than mid-century Swiss grotesques. Old-style figures ship as default, spacing is loose enough for comfortable text reading, and the italic is properly drawn rather than slanted. Nine weights with matching italics make it as useful in editorial hierarchies as it is in body text.
foundry_blurb: Klim describes National as a deceptively simple sans serif whose subtle quirks give it a distinctive but not distracting personality. Drawn from the Akzidenz Grotesk era, it has a humble, workmanlike character with an agreeable tone of voice, designed for long-form reading at small sizes.

name: National 2
classification_notes: Modern grotesque drawing on pre-Akzidenz-Grotesk references. Clean, regularised letterforms with restrained personality and workmanlike proportions. Available in four widths spanning from text to compressed display use. Lining numerals default with old-style figures via OpenType.
summary: Kris Sowersby's decade-long reworking of his 2007 original, expanding a pre-Akzidenz grotesque across four widths and eight weights with every letterform redrawn for cleaner curves and better weight distribution.
description: National 2 is Kris Sowersby's full redraw of the original National, released in 2017 after ten years of refinement. Every letterform was redrawn to improve curve quality and stroke distribution, with three new width variants – Narrow, Condensed and Compressed – added to extend the family's range. Its debt to pre-Akzidenz-Grotesk gives it a grounded, functional character suited to both body text and headline work.
foundry_blurb: National 2 is a complete overhaul of Klim's popular National sans, 10 years in the making, with every letter redrawn and remastered. Weight distribution is improved, curves are refined, and three new widths – Narrow, Condensed and Compressed – join the original to make 64 fonts in total. National's details are drawn from the era of Akzidenz-Grotesk, giving it a humble, workmanlike character with an agreeable tone of voice.

name: National 2 Compressed
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Modern: Lineal/Grotesque; the tightest of three new widths added in the 10-year overhaul of National, drawing details from the era of Akzidenz-Grotesk for a humble, workmanlike character.
summary: The tightest width in the National 2 system, an Akzidenz-rooted grotesque drawn for headlines and dense column setting.
description: The compressed cut of National 2 by Kris Sowersby, the tightest of three new widths added in the 10-year overhaul of National. Sixteen styles run from Thin to Black with matching italics, all redrawn and remastered with refined curves and better weight distribution. Sits inside the wider National 2 system alongside National 2, Narrow and Condensed, so the same Akzidenz-era voice carries from running text into very tight headlines.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify National 2 Compressed as Modern: Lineal/Grotesque, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2017. They describe National 2 as a complete overhaul of National, ten years in the making, with every letter redrawn and three new widths (Narrow, Condensed and Compressed). The details are drawn from the era of Akzidenz-Grotesk, giving it a humble, workmanlike character.

name: National 2 Condensed
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Modern: Lineal/Grotesque; one of three new widths in the 10-year overhaul of National, sitting between Narrow and Compressed, with details drawn from the era of Akzidenz-Grotesk.
summary: The middle condensed width of the National 2 system, a redrawn Akzidenz-rooted grotesque for tight columns and headlines.
description: The condensed cut of National 2 by Kris Sowersby, sitting between Narrow and Compressed in the redrawn National 2 system. Sixteen styles run from Thin to Black with paired italics, with every letter remastered, refined curves and improved weight distribution. The Akzidenz-era detailing keeps the voice humble and workmanlike at small sizes, while the condensed proportions earn their place in editorial headlines, social design and wayfinding.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify National 2 Condensed as Modern: Lineal/Grotesque, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2017. They describe National 2 as a complete overhaul of National, ten years in the making, with every letter redrawn and three new widths (Narrow, Condensed and Compressed) added. The details come from the era of Akzidenz-Grotesk, giving the family a humble, workmanlike character.

name: National 2 Narrow
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Modern: Lineal/Grotesque; the widest of the three new condensed widths added in the 10-year overhaul of National, drawing on Akzidenz-Grotesk era detailing.
summary: The narrow cut of National 2, a gently tightened Akzidenz-rooted grotesque for editorial and brand work where space is short.
description: The narrow cut of National 2 by Kris Sowersby, the widest of the three condensed widths added in the redrawn National 2 system. Sixteen styles run from Thin to Black with paired italics, redrawn and remastered with cleaner curves and better weight distribution. Sits well in editorial and brand work that needs a slightly tighter sans without going as compact as Condensed or Compressed, while keeping the family's Akzidenz-era detailing intact.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify National 2 Narrow as Modern: Lineal/Grotesque, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2017. They describe National 2 as a complete overhaul of National, ten years in the making, with every letter redrawn and three new widths (Narrow, Condensed and Compressed) added. Its details are drawn from the era of Akzidenz-Grotesk, giving it a humble, workmanlike character.

name: Newzald
classification_notes: Transitional serif with Dutch baroque influences from J.F. Rosart and J.M. Fleischman. Large x-height and slightly condensed proportions optimised for editorial column setting. Klim classifies it as Modern: Transitional/Realist.
summary: An editorial text face drawing from Dutch baroque punchcutters Rosart and Fleischman, with a large x-height and slightly condensed forms built for dense column setting.
description: Newzald takes its cues from J.F. Rosart and J.M. Fleischman, 18th-century Dutch punchcutters known for their economical rigour. The large x-height and subtly condensed proportions let it carry many words per column without looking cramped. Released in 2008, it is a capable workhorse for newspaper and magazine text environments, offered in four weights each with a roman and italic.
foundry_blurb: Klim describes Newzald as a hardworking text typeface for the international editorial environment. Its large x-height and slightly condensed forms allow high word counts per column without sacrificing readability, drawing aesthetic inspiration from the classic Dutch types of Rosart and Fleischman.

name: Pitch
classification_notes: Classified by Klim as "Moderns: Mechanistic/Slab Serif Monospace." Fixed-width throughout, with monoline strokes that disregard optical correction, flat angular brackets connecting stems to slabs, and ball terminals inherited from Sowersby's earlier Darling. Weight progression is linear to simulate ink pressure variation rather than conventional optical adjustment.
summary: A monospaced slab serif that distils typewriter aesthetics into digital form, evoking ink pressure and mechanical warmth through linear weight progression and flat angular brackets rather than literal distressing.
description: Designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2012, Pitch uses fixed-width spacing as its defining condition, matching Courier's 10-pitch set width and drawing on the letterform vocabulary of vintage Remington and Underwood machines. Monoline strokes, flat angular slab brackets and ball terminals simulate ink spread across a linear weight progression, while the italic references Bauer's Schreibmaschinenschrift specimen. A sans serif companion, Pitch Sans, followed in 2018 with the serifs stripped but the mechanical character preserved through small flat terminals at stroke joins.
foundry_blurb: Klim describes Pitch as a synthesis of digital and analogue that evokes rather than emulates typewritten text. Matching Courier's 10-pitch set width, it captures the warmth of writing machines through linear weight progression and ink-spread simulation without artificial distressing. The collection received the Australian Design Biennale Judge's Choice and Tokyo TDC recognition.

name: Pitch Sans
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Modern: Lineal/Sans Serif Monospace; a typewriter-inspired sans monospace, sibling to Pitch, described as a synthesis of digital and analogue that evokes typewritten text rather than emulating it.
summary: A sans monospace that evokes typewritten text without imitating it, sibling to the slab-serif Pitch.
description: A monospaced sans by Kris Sowersby, the sans companion to Pitch, drawn as a love letter to the typewriter rather than a literal revival. Five weights run from Light to Bold with paired italics, all on the same fixed advance width, so it locks into code, captions and tabular settings cleanly. Sits comfortably in editorial and tech work that wants a typewriter atmosphere without the worn-ribbon pastiche.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Pitch Sans as Modern: Lineal/Sans Serif Monospace, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2018. They describe Pitch as a love letter to the typewriter, a synthesis of digital and analogue that evokes typewritten text rather than emulating it. Pitch Sans is the sans-serif sibling within the wider Pitch collection.

name: Signifier
classification_notes: Drawn from the 17th-century Fell Types held at Oxford University Press – the English Roman attributed to Nicolaes Briot (c.1670s, ~13.5pt) and the italic from Granjon's Pica Italic – but recast as a digital Brutalist work rather than a conventional revival. Sowersby deliberately deleted curves, snapped details to grids and embraced interpolation artefacts in lighter weights. Rectangular baseline serifs, triangular head serifs (referencing Licko's Matrix, 1986) and Matthew Carter-influenced chopped terminals define the texture. Available as a variable font (weight axis 100–900). Klim classifies it internally as Modern Oldstyle. Red Dot Grand Prix winner 2021.
summary: A Brutalist response to the 17th-century Fell Types, Sowersby recasts their letterforms in ones and zeros by embracing machine logic over analogue mimicry.
description: Signifier draws on the English Roman from Oxford's Fell Types – cut in the 1670s and attributed to Nicolaes Briot – and Granjon's Pica Italic, but pursues no conventional revival. Sowersby worked deliberately with the computer, snapping details to grids and embracing interpolation artefacts in lighter weights to produce letterforms that acknowledge the nature of digital type. Sharp triangular head serifs, rectangular baseline serifs and Charter-inflected chopped terminals give it a distinctive precision that holds from text to display sizes.
foundry_blurb: Klim describe Signifier as a Brutalist response to 17th-century typefaces, with its digital immateriality drawing on a deeply material past. Sowersby worked consciously with the computer to recast the lead, antimony and tin of the Fell Types into ones and zeros, allowing Bézier curves and sharp vectors determined by machine logic to define the result. The design acknowledges that what once was infinitely variable is now infinitely repeatable.

name: Söhne
classification_notes: Neo-grotesque drawn from the analogue memory of Akzidenz-Grotesk – specifically Standard Medium as used in Unimark's NYC Subway wayfinding system – and recast through Helvetica's proportions. Designed outward from the Halbfett weight rather than a regular. Default 'a' carries a tail; an alternate double-storey 'g' is included, both drawing on related historical grotesks including Breede Halfvette Antieke and Blockschrift. Low contrast, tight spacing, angled terminals.
summary: A neo-grotesque drawn from the memory of Akzidenz-Grotesk as used in the NYC Subway, recast through Helvetica's proportions by Kris Sowersby in 2019.
description: Söhne was designed outward from Akzidenz-Grotesk's Halbfett rather than a regular weight, capturing the tight spacing, low contrast and angled terminals of mid-century subway signage without attempting a literal revival. The family spans eight weights with italics across four sub-families: a standard cut, a wide Breit, a condensed Schmal, and a Mono variant that adds serifs to narrow characters to maintain legibility at fixed pitch. It won the Red Dot Award Best of the Best in Typography in 2020 and has become one of the defining grotesques of the digital era.
foundry_blurb: Klim describe Söhne as the memory of Akzidenz-Grotesk framed through the reality of Helvetica, drawing on the analogue materiality of Standard Medium as deployed in Unimark's 1970 NYC Transit Graphics Standards Manual. The family was designed outward from the Halbfett weight and incorporates alternate glyphs from related historical grotesks including Breede Halfvette Antieke and Blockschrift.

name: Söhne Breit
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Lineal: Grotesque; the wide cut in the Söhne system, capturing the analogue materiality of Standard Medium used in Unimark's NYC Subway wayfinding.
summary: The wide cut of Söhne, holding the family's Akzidenz-meets-Helvetica neutrality at expansive proportions for display and branding.
description: The wide companion to Söhne, drawn by Kris Sowersby with the same Akzidenz-Grotesk and Standard Medium reference points stretched horizontally. Eight weights from Extraleicht to Extrafett run with matching Kursiv italics, giving the same German weight nomenclature as the parent family. Brands reach for it when headlines need width and air without tipping into a true display face, often paired back with Söhne or Söhne Mono for body text.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Söhne Breit as Lineal: Grotesque, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2019. They describe Söhne as the memory of Akzidenz-Grotesk seen through the reality of Helvetica, capturing the analogue materiality of Standard Medium used in Unimark's NYC Subway wayfinding.

name: Söhne Mono
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Lineal: Grotesque, Monospaced; the fixed-width cut in the Söhne system, sharing the Akzidenz-Grotesk lineage of the parent family.
summary: A grotesque monospace tied to the Söhne system, giving fixed-width text the same Akzidenz lineage as its proportional sibling.
description: The monospaced cut in the Söhne system by Kris Sowersby, sharing the parent family's Akzidenz-Grotesk reference and Standard Medium tone. Eight weights with Kursiv italics give a fuller weight ladder than most code fonts offer, and stylistic alternates handle the alternate a and g for designers wanting to soften the grotesque feel. Used for code, data UI and editorial captions where the rest of the system already runs on Söhne.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Söhne Mono as Lineal: Grotesque, Monospaced, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2019. They describe Söhne as the memory of Akzidenz-Grotesk seen through the reality of Helvetica, capturing the analogue materiality of Standard Medium used in Unimark's NYC Subway wayfinding.

name: Söhne Schmal
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Lineal: Grotesque; the condensed cut in the Söhne system, drawn from the same Akzidenz-Grotesk and Standard Medium reference points as the parent family.
summary: The condensed cut of Söhne, taking the Akzidenz lineage into tight columns and stacked headlines without losing the family's neutrality.
description: The narrow companion to Söhne, drawn by Kris Sowersby for measures and stacked headlines that the standard width can't hold. Eight weights from Extraleicht to Extrafett run with Kursiv italics, keeping the Söhne family's eight-step German nomenclature consistent across widths. Editorial mastheads, posters and tight UI labels are the natural home, often paired with Söhne for body copy.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Söhne Schmal as Lineal: Grotesque, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2019. They describe Söhne as the memory of Akzidenz-Grotesk seen through the reality of Helvetica, capturing the analogue materiality of Standard Medium used in Unimark's NYC Subway wayfinding.

name: The Future
classification_notes: Geometric sans-serif modelled on Paul Renner's Futura. Sowersby worked from original brass plates and intaglio prints at the Museum für Druckkunst Leipzig to restore Futura's early, stricter geometric construction — purer circular forms, weight-specific optical corrections, and a selection of Renner's experimental alternates (ten stylistic sets). The accompanying The Future Mono is a speculative monospaced variant framed as a typewriter adaptation under Japanese typographic influence, featuring outlined punctuation and the eccentric stick-and-ball r alternate.
summary: A rigorous geometric sans built from Renner's original Futura production drawings, paired with a speculative monospaced companion reimagined as a typewriter face.
description: The Future is Kris Sowersby's close study of Paul Renner's Futura, developed from original brass plates and intaglio prints at the Museum für Druckkunst Leipzig. It restores the stricter geometric severity of early Futura iterations while retaining the weight-specific optical corrections and eccentric alternates that give Renner's work its character. The Future Mono extends the family as a speculative monospaced variant, framing Futura as if adapted by Renner for typewriter use under Japanese typographic influence, with outlined punctuation and an unusual stick-and-ball r.
foundry_blurb: Klim describes The Future as a homage to Futura that returns to Renner's original geometric ambitions, drawing on primary source material to recover a stricter, more abstract version of the typeface than the one that became commercially ubiquitous. The Future Mono is presented as a speculative commission by Kyota Sugimoto, asking what Futura might look like remade for a monospaced, typewriter context.

name: The Future Mono
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Monospaced geometric sans-serif; a speculative reimagining of Futura as a typewriter font commissioned by Kyota Sugimoto, sitting alongside The Future as a homage to Paul Renner's geometric classic.
summary: A geometric monospace by Kris Sowersby that imagines Futura as a typewriter face, with seven weights and a deep stylistic alternates set.
description: A geometric monospace by Kris Sowersby drawn as a speculative pairing for The Future, treating Futura as if it had been cut for a typewriter rather than for advertising. Seven weights from Thin to Black run with italics, and the OpenType set carries fifteen stylistic sets covering alt a, g, h, m, n, r, u and square forms borrowed from Renner's avant-garde alternates. Reads cleanly in code and captions, then turns expressive when the alternates are switched on for posters or art direction.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify The Future Mono as Monospaced geometric sans-serif, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2022. They describe it as a speculative take that reimagines Futura as a typewriter font commissioned by Kyota Sugimoto, alongside The Future, their homage to Paul Renner's progressive classic.

name: Tiempos Fine
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Modern: Transitional/Realist; the sharpest optical size in the Tiempos system, keeping the proportions and letterfit of Tiempos Headline while intensifying the interplay between warm curves and sharp details.
summary: The sharpest optical cut in the Tiempos system, with high contrast and crisp terminals tuned for large editorial and fashion headlines.
description: The display optical size in the Tiempos system, drawn by Kris Sowersby and Noe Blanco. Six weights from Light to Black with italics keep the proportions and letterfit of Tiempos Headline, then push contrast and terminal sharpness for use at the largest sizes. A weight-axis variable font is supplied with the full family. Editorial covers, fashion mastheads and luxury display work where Tiempos Headline starts to feel slightly soft.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Tiempos Fine as Modern: Transitional/Realist, designed by Kris Sowersby and Noe Blanco and released in 2018. They describe it as the Fine size in the Tiempos system, keeping the proportions and letterfit of Tiempos Headline while intensifying the interplay between warm curves and sharp details.

name: Tiempos Headline
classification_notes: Modern Transitional/Realist serif tracing its lineage through Plantin and Times New Roman via Kris Sowersby's earlier Galaxie Copernicus. Tiempos Text originated as an optimisation for a Spanish newspaper redesign and later became a standalone family. Headline is the display-size cut: tighter letterfit, higher stroke contrast, and sharper terminal details than the Text sibling. Tiempos Fine (2018) pushes the contrast and refinement further still. Overall classification sits between Transitional and Realist – mechanically constructed but with warm humanist curves.
summary: A hardworking editorial serif in the Plantin–Times tradition, optimised for display sizes with tight letterfit and a tension between warm curves and sharp details.
description: Tiempos Headline is the display-size cut of Klim's Tiempos family, a modern transitional serif tracing its lineage through Plantin and Times New Roman. Sowersby originally developed Tiempos Text for a Spanish newspaper redesign, refining the letterfit, spacing and italic angle to suit economic typesetting at text sizes; Headline takes those proportions and snaps them tighter for large-scale use, amplifying stroke contrast and sharpening the details. The family rounds out with Tiempos Fine (2018), a more refined display cut co-designed with Noe Blanco, which intensifies the contrast further for use in luxury editorial contexts like National Geographic Magazine.
foundry_blurb: Klim describes Tiempos as a hardworking modern serif for editorial typography that takes the functionality of Plantin and Times and updates it for contemporary use. The Headline cut is calibrated for larger sizes, built on the same proportions and letterfit as Tiempos Fine while emphasising the interplay of warm curves and sharp details. The full collection – Text, Headline, Fine – spans body copy through display work, each cut optically corrected for its intended size range.

name: Tiempos Text
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Modern: Transitional/Realist; takes the functionality of Plantin and Times and updates it for contemporary, economical typesetting.
summary: A workhorse text serif drawing on Plantin and Times, tuned for legible, economical body copy in editorial and news settings.
description: A pragmatic transitional serif by Kris Sowersby that updates the Plantin and Times News Roman lineage for contemporary, economical typesetting. The Tiempos system runs across three optical sizes (Text, Headline, Fine), so the same family carries you from body copy to mastheads without breaking voice. Reads quiet at small sizes and steady at large, which is why news, longform and editorial brands reach for it when the serif needs to stay out of the way.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Tiempos Text as Modern: Transitional/Realist, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2010. They describe it as Plantin and Times reimagined for present-day, space-efficient text setting, sitting at the Text size in the wider Tiempos system alongside Headline and Fine.

name: Untitled Sans
classification_notes: Modern lineal neo-grotesque. Designed to carry no individual stylistic signature — references Akzidenz Grotesk (straight R leg, teardrop 'a') and Helvetica (90° terminals on C, r, s) without calling on either directly. Conceptually rooted in Jasper Morrison and Naoto Fukasawa's Super Normal project. Evolved from an internal project called "National Plain" (begun c. 2009), a stripped-back variant of Sowersby's National.
summary: A deliberately unassuming neo-grotesque from Kris Sowersby, designed to carry no individual designer's signature — the typographic equivalent of Jasper Morrison's Super Normal.
description: Released in 2017, Untitled Sans draws on early grotesque references — Akzidenz Grotesk's straight leg and Helvetica's 90° terminals — without announcing either influence. Loose spacing and stripped-back forms produce a quiet, functional presence suited to contexts that demand neutrality over character. Available in five weights with italics and as a variable font (weight axis 300–900), it sits alongside Untitled Serif as part of Klim's Untitled Collection. It won the Tokyo TDC Annual Award in 2019.
foundry_blurb: Klim describes Untitled Sans as a plain neogrotesk validated by the Super Normal project — a collaboration between Jasper Morrison and Naoto Fukasawa exploring how the most useful objects appear designed by no one in particular. Sowersby approached the design with deliberate detachment, avoiding personal stylistic flourishes to produce something ordinary and quietly useful.

name: Untitled Serif
classification_notes: Klim classifies it as Modern: Garalde/Oldstyle; drawn from the post-Caslon, pre-Times workhorses of metal type, sharing Untitled Sans's Super Normal concept rather than a shared skeleton.
summary: A quotidian old-style serif drawn from post-Caslon metal workhorses, paired by concept with Untitled Sans for plain, readable text.
description: An old-style serif by Kris Sowersby drawn from the post-Caslon, pre-Times workhorses that nearly every metal foundry once offered, then quietened in the spirit of Morrison and Fukasawa's Super Normal. Three weights (Regular, Medium, Bold) with italics keep the family lean, and a variable weight axis is supplied with the full family. Pairs by concept with Untitled Sans, and works for editorial body, books and brands that want a serif with no obvious authorial signature.
foundry_blurb: Klim classify Untitled Serif as Modern: Garalde/Oldstyle, designed by Kris Sowersby and released in 2017. They describe it as drawn from the post-Caslon, pre-Times workhorses offered by almost every metal foundry of the time, paired with Untitled Sans by concept rather than skeleton, with a deliberate aesthetic of not being designed by anyone in particular.
